title: Pressure, Winds, Storms, and Cyclones
subject: Science
description: Pressure as force per unit area, pressure in liquids and the atmosphere, how pressure differences create winds and breezes, and how storms, thunderstorms, lightning and cyclones form and can be survived.

questions.question: Megha and Pawan carry equally heavy bags, but only Pawan's bag hurts his shoulders. Why?
options: His bag has narrow straps, so the weight acts on a smaller area
His bag has longer straps, so the weight hangs further down
His bag is packed with heavier items than his sister's bag
His bag has broad straps, so the weight spreads over more skin
questions.explanation: Both bags weigh the same, but Pawan's narrow straps press the weight onto a smaller area of the shoulder, giving a higher pressure. Broad straps (Megha's) spread the same force over a larger area.

questions.question: How does the chapter define pressure?
options: The force multiplied by the area
The force acting per unit area
The area acted on per unit force
The weight acting per unit volume
questions.explanation: Pressure = Force ÷ Area, i.e. force per unit area. Multiplying force by area or dividing area by force are the common slips.

questions.question: Two bags have the same weight; one has broad straps and the other narrow straps. Which quantity is the SAME for both and which is DIFFERENT?
options: Same force and same pressure on the shoulder
Same pressure on the shoulder; different force
Same force on the shoulder; different pressure
Different force and different pressure
questions.explanation: The force (weight of the bag) is identical. Because the area of contact differs, the pressure (force ÷ area) differs — larger for narrow straps.

questions.question: People carrying pots on their heads place a round piece of cloth under the load. What does the cloth do?
options: It cools the head so that the carrier does not feel the heavy load
It reduces the weight of the pot by absorbing part of the load
It increases friction so that the pot does not slip off the head
It increases the area over which the weight acts, lowering pressure
questions.explanation: The cloth ring spreads the same weight over a larger area of the head, so the pressure is reduced. The weight itself does not change.

questions.question: Why is it easier to lift a full bucket by a broad handle than by a narrow one?
options: The broad handle makes the water inside the bucket weigh less
The broad handle spreads the force over a larger area of the hand
The broad handle shifts the water towards the centre of the bucket
The broad handle lets the hand grip with a much larger force
questions.explanation: The weight of the bucket is unchanged; a broad handle puts that force on a larger area of the palm, so the pressure felt is smaller.

questions.question: Which statement about pressure is NOT correct?
options: Two equal forces can produce different pressures on a surface
Halving the area over which a force acts doubles the pressure
Pressure is a quantity that depends on both force and area
Doubling the area over which a force acts doubles the pressure
questions.explanation: Pressure = force ÷ area, so doubling the area HALVES the pressure. The other three statements follow directly from the definition.

questions.question: A person of the same weight walks on soft snow once in boots and once on wide skis. Using the chapter's idea, which is true?
options: Both exert equal pressure because the weight is equal
Skis exert more pressure, so the person sinks more
Skis exert less pressure, so the person sinks less
Boots exert less pressure because they are smaller
questions.explanation: Same weight, larger area → smaller pressure. Wide skis spread the weight over more snow, so the person sinks less — the same reasoning as broad bag straps.

questions.question: A force of 100 N acts on a board. If the same force is now applied on half the area, the pressure becomes
options: twice as large
half as large
the same
four times as large
questions.explanation: Pressure = force ÷ area. Halving the area with the force fixed doubles the pressure.

questions.question: Pressure increases when the same force acts over a larger area.
questions.explanation: It is the opposite: spreading the same force over a larger area decreases the pressure (force ÷ area).

questions.question: In this chapter, pressure is computed only for forces that act perpendicular to the surface.
questions.explanation: The chapter states that at this stage only forces acting perpendicular to the surface are considered when computing pressure.

questions.question: Pressure and force are two names for the same physical quantity.
questions.explanation: Force is a push or pull; pressure is force per unit area. The same force can give very different pressures depending on the area.

questions.question: Which of these REDUCE the pressure produced by a given force? (Select all that apply.)
options: Broad straps on a school bag
The pointed tip of an iron nail
A round cloth placed under a pot carried on the head
The sharp edge of a kitchen knife
questions.explanation: Broad straps and the cloth ring increase the contact area, lowering pressure. A pointed tip and a sharp edge do the opposite — they shrink the area to raise pressure.

questions.question: Megha says: 'My bag feels lighter because of its broad straps.' Which correction is scientifically accurate?
options: The bag is not lighter; the force on your shoulders is lower
The bag is lighter because broad straps carry part of the weight
The bag is lighter because gravity acts less on broad straps
The bag is not lighter; the pressure on your shoulders is lower
questions.explanation: Weight (force) is unchanged — gravity acts the same. What changes is the pressure, because the force is spread over a larger area.

questions.question: What is the SI unit of pressure?
options: newton per cubic metre (N/m³), also called a torr
newton per metre (N/m), also called a bar
newton per square metre (N/m²), also called pascal
kilogram per square metre (kg/m²), also called a pascal
questions.explanation: Force is in newton and area in metre², so pressure is N/m², which is named the pascal (Pa).

questions.question: A force of 100 N is applied on a cardboard of area 2 m². The pressure on the cardboard is
options: 200 N/m²
50 N/m²
100 N/m²
questions.explanation: Pressure = 100 N ÷ 2 m² = 50 N/m² (50 Pa). Multiplying (200) and forgetting to divide (100) are common slips.

questions.question: One millibar (mb), the practical unit of air pressure, equals
options: 100 Pa
10 Pa
1 Pa
questions.explanation: The 'A step further' box states that 1 millibar = 100 pascal; it is also equal to 1 hectopascal (hPa).

questions.question: How are the millibar (mb) and the hectopascal (hPa) related?
options: 1 hPa = 10 mb, since 1 mb is 10 Pa
1 mb = 10 hPa, since 1 hPa is 10 Pa
1 mb = 1 hPa, both being 100 Pa
1 mb = 100 hPa, since 1 hPa is 1 Pa
questions.explanation: Both the millibar and the hectopascal are defined as 100 Pa, so they are equal units.

questions.question: An elephant of weight 20000 N stands on four feet, each of area 0.25 m². The pressure on the ground is
questions.explanation: Total area = 4 × 0.25 = 1 m². Pressure = 20000 N ÷ 1 m² = 20000 Pa. Using only one foot's area gives 80000 Pa (wrong); dividing by 4 gives 5000 Pa (wrong).

questions.question: The same 20000 N elephant lifts one foot off the ground. The pressure on the ground now becomes about
questions.explanation: Area is now 3 × 0.25 = 0.75 m². Pressure = 20000 ÷ 0.75 ≈ 26667 Pa — higher than before because the same weight acts on less area.

questions.question: Boat A (base 7 m²) carries 5 persons; boat B (base 3.5 m²) carries 3 persons. Each person weighs 700 N. Which boat has more pressure on its base, and by how much?
options: Boat A, by 100 Pa
Boat B, by 100 Pa
Boat B, by 1400 Pa
Both are equal in pressure
questions.explanation: A: 5 × 700 = 3500 N ÷ 7 m² = 500 Pa. B: 3 × 700 = 2100 N ÷ 3.5 m² = 600 Pa. B is higher by 100 Pa even though A carries more total weight.

questions.question: In the two-boat problem, boat A carries the larger total weight (3500 N) yet has the lower pressure. This happens because
options: its weight is spread over twice the base area of boat B
its persons sit nearer the centre, reducing the pressure
pressure depends on the number of persons, not weight
water pushes up more strongly on a larger boat base
questions.explanation: Pressure = force ÷ area. Boat A's base (7 m²) is double boat B's (3.5 m²), so even with more force its pressure (500 Pa) is below B's (600 Pa).

questions.question: Since the SI unit of force is the newton and that of area is the square metre, the SI unit of pressure is newton per square metre.
questions.explanation: Pressure = force ÷ area, so its unit is N/m², which is also called the pascal.

questions.question: One hectopascal is equal to 1000 pascal.
questions.explanation: Hecto- means 100, so 1 hPa = 100 Pa (the same as 1 millibar).

questions.question: The chapter says the air column above a 15 cm × 15 cm area pushes with about 2250 N. The atmospheric pressure this implies is roughly
options: 50 Pa
questions.explanation: Area = 0.15 m × 0.15 m = 0.0225 m². Pressure = 2250 N ÷ 0.0225 m² = 100000 Pa (about 1000 mb). Using 225 cm² without converting gives a wrong answer.

questions.question: Which of these unit statements are correct? (Select all that apply.)
options: 1 Pa = 1 N/m²
1 mb = 100 Pa
1 hPa = 10 mb
1 mb = 100 hPa
questions.explanation: A pascal is one newton per square metre and a millibar is 100 Pa. Since 1 hPa is also 100 Pa, 1 hPa = 1 mb — not 10 mb or 1/100 mb.

questions.question: What force must act on an area of 4 m² to produce a pressure of 50 Pa?
questions.explanation: Force = pressure × area = 50 Pa × 4 m² = 200 N. Dividing instead of multiplying gives 12.5 N.

questions.question: A force of 2250 N acts on 15 cm × 15 cm. If the same force acted on 30 cm × 30 cm instead, the pressure would be
options: four times as much
half as much
twice as much
one quarter as much
questions.explanation: Doubling both sides makes the area four times larger (0.09 m² instead of 0.0225 m²), so the pressure falls to one quarter. 'Half' is the tempting slip.

questions.question: It is easier to drive an iron nail into wood by its pointed end because
options: the pointed tip is heavier and so pushes down harder
the small area of the tip produces a very high pressure
the tip is smoother and so has less friction with wood
the tip is made of a harder metal than the head of the nail
questions.explanation: The same hammer force acting on the tiny tip area gives a very large pressure, which pierces the wood. The head, with a large area, gives low pressure.

questions.question: Why does the sharp edge of a knife cut an apple more easily than the blunt edge?
options: The sharp edge has more friction with the skin of the apple
The sharp edge applies a bigger force than the blunt edge
The sharp edge is heavier, so gravity helps it cut downwards
The sharp edge has a smaller area, so the pressure is greater
questions.explanation: The force applied by the hand is the same; a thin edge concentrates it on a very small area, so the pressure is high enough to cut.

questions.question: A boy lies horizontally on a loose sand bed and then stands vertically on it. In which case does he sink more, and why?
options: Both equally — his weight is the same, so the pressure is the same
Lying — his whole body pushes on the sand, so the total force is larger
Standing — his weight acts on a much smaller area, so pressure is higher
Lying — the sand grains spread out more easily under a long body
questions.explanation: The weight is the same in both cases. Standing puts it on only the area of the feet, so pressure is much higher and he sinks more. Lying spreads it over a large area.

questions.question: Which statement about the nail-and-knife activities in Table 6.1 is NOT correct?
options: The blunt knife edge is easier to cut with because it is wider
The pointed end of a nail is easier to drive in than its head
A smaller area for the same force gives a higher pressure
The sharp edge of a knife cuts an apple more easily than the blunt edge
questions.explanation: A blunt (wider) edge spreads the force over more area, giving lower pressure — so it is HARDER to cut with. The other statements match the activity conclusions.

questions.question: A blunt knife needs more effort than a sharp one because its wider edge spreads the force over a larger area, lowering the pressure.
questions.explanation: Pressure = force ÷ area. A wider edge means more area and so less pressure for the same force, making cutting difficult.

questions.question: Driving a nail by its flat head is easier than by its pointed end because the head has more area.
questions.explanation: More area means LESS pressure for the same force, so the head is harder to drive in. The pointed end, with tiny area, gives high pressure.

questions.question: Which design feature INCREASES the pressure produced by a given force?
options: The round cloth under a head load
The broad handle of a water bucket
The broad strap of a school bag
The pointed tip of an iron nail
questions.explanation: Only the pointed tip reduces the area, which raises pressure. The other three enlarge the area to reduce pressure.

questions.question: A drawing pin has a flat head on the thumb side and a sharp point on the board side. Pressing it, the force on both ends is the same. Why does only the point go in?
options: The head is made of plastic, which cannot cut into the thumb
The thumb pushes with a smaller force than the board pushes back
The point has tiny area, so its pressure on the board is very high
The board is softer than the thumb and so gets pierced first
questions.explanation: Same force, two very different areas: the broad head gives low pressure on the thumb; the sharp point gives huge pressure on the board, so it pierces.

questions.question: Which of these work by DECREASING area to INCREASE pressure? (Select all that apply.)
options: A sharp knife edge
The pointed end of a nail
Broad bag straps
A cloth ring under a pot
questions.explanation: Knife edges and nail points shrink the area so the same force gives high pressure. Straps and cloth rings do the reverse.

questions.question: What single conclusion do the observations in Table 6.1 (nail and knife) lead to?
options: A larger area for a given force gives higher pressure, making some tasks easier
A smaller area for a given force gives higher pressure, making some tasks easier
Heavier tools always do a task more easily than lighter tools
Sharp tools apply a larger force on an object than blunt tools
questions.explanation: The chapter concludes that when the area over which a force acts is smaller, the pressure is higher, so driving a nail by its tip or cutting with a sharp edge is easier.

questions.question: The standing boy sinks more into sand than the lying boy. If he now stands on one foot, what happens compared with standing on two?
options: He sinks even more, since the same weight acts on half the area
He sinks the same, since his weight has not changed at all
He sinks less, since one foot pushes the sand grains apart less
He sinks even more, since standing on one foot increases his weight
questions.explanation: His weight is unchanged, but the contact area halves, so the pressure doubles and he sinks further.

questions.question: In Activity 6.1, two pipes of different diameters with balloons at the bottom are filled with water to the same height. What is observed?
options: The balloon on the narrow pipe bulges much more
The balloon on the broad pipe bulges much more
Both balloons bulge to the same extent
Neither balloon bulges because water is light
questions.explanation: Equal water-column heights produce equal bulges despite different diameters — showing that pressure depends on the height of the column.

questions.question: In Activity 6.1 the broad pipe holds more water than the narrow pipe, yet both balloons bulge equally. What does this tell us?
options: The weight of water is not what decides the bulge; the column height is
The weight of water decides the bulge, and the two weights happen to be equal
Balloons stretch by a fixed amount no matter what presses on them
The narrow pipe squeezes the water, making up for its smaller weight
questions.explanation: Since the weights differ but the bulges are equal, weight cannot be the cause. The pressure exerted by the water column, which depends on its height, is.

questions.question: More water is poured into one pipe in Activity 6.1. What happens to the balloon at its bottom?
options: It bulges more, because the water becomes heavier per litre
It bulges less, because the extra water presses the sides more
It stays the same, because the pipe's diameter has not changed
It bulges more, because the pressure rises with column height
questions.explanation: The bulge increases as the water column grows taller: pressure at the bottom of a liquid rises with the height of the column.

questions.question: Why are overhead water tanks placed at a height?
options: Water at a height stays cooler and cleaner than water at ground level
A taller water column gives more pressure, so taps give a good stream
A high tank holds more water than the same tank kept on the ground
Water at a height is lighter, so it flows through pipes more easily
questions.explanation: The pressure exerted by a liquid depends on the height of its column. A high tank gives a tall column and hence higher pressure at the taps.

questions.question: A tank is on the top floor of a three-storeyed building. You live on the second floor; your friend lives on the first floor. Who gets the more powerful tap stream?
options: Your friend, since the water column above the first floor is taller
You, since the second floor is closer to the tank's outlet pipe
Both equally, since the same tank supplies both the floors
You, since less pipe length means less loss of pressure
questions.explanation: Pressure depends on the height of the water column above the tap. The first floor is lower, so its column is taller and its pressure is greater.

questions.question: A tank sits on a roof at height H. To get water with MORE pressure on the ground floor, one has to
options: decrease the height H at which the tank is placed
increase the height H at which the tank is placed
replace it with a tank of the same height holding more water
replace it with a tank of the same height holding less water
questions.explanation: Liquid pressure depends on the height of the column, not on how much water the tank holds. Raising H increases pressure at the ground-floor tap.

questions.question: Someone suggests replacing a rooftop tank with a wider tank of the same height to get stronger tap pressure. Why will this NOT work?
options: A wider tank is heavier and would press the water back up the pipes
A wider tank spreads the water out, so the pressure at the taps falls
Pressure depends on the water-column height, not on the tank's width or volume
A wider tank holds more water, so the pressure would be too high to use
questions.explanation: The bulging-balloon activity showed that only the height of the water column matters. Same height means same pressure, however wide the tank.

questions.question: In Activity 6.2, water flows out of holes made on the SIDES of a bottle near its bottom. This shows that
options: water always flows upward when a container has holes
liquids exert pressure only at the bottom of their container
air pushes the water out through the holes in the bottle
liquids exert pressure on the walls of their container
questions.explanation: Water spurting sideways shows that the liquid pushes on the sides of the container — liquids exert pressure in all directions, not just downward.

questions.question: Predict: a bottle has three holes, one near the bottom, one in the middle and one near the top. When filled, which jet travels farthest?
options: The jet from the hole near the top
The jet from the hole near the bottom
The jet from the hole in the middle
All three jets travel equally far
questions.explanation: Liquid pressure increases with the height of the water column above a point. The lowest hole has the tallest column above it, so the highest pressure and the strongest jet.

questions.question: Vessels A and B are filled with water to the same level; B has a broader base than A. P is the pressure and F the force of water at the base. Then
options: P_A > P_B and F_A > F_B
P_A = P_B and F_A = F_B
P_A < P_B and F_A = F_B
P_A = P_B and F_A < F_B
questions.explanation: Same height ⇒ same pressure at the base. Force = pressure × area, and B's base is larger, so the force on B's base is greater.

questions.question: Three vessels P, Q and R of different shapes are connected at their bases. Water is poured into R and pouring is stopped. The water level will be
options: highest in vessel P
highest in vessel R
equal in all three vessels
highest in vessel Q
questions.explanation: Liquid pressure depends only on column height. Water flows between the connected vessels until the pressure (and hence the level) is the same in all of them, whatever their shapes.

questions.question: Why is the base of a dam made much broader than its top?
options: The horizontal water pressure is very large near the bottom
The water is coldest near the bottom and expands the wall
More water is stored near the top than near the bottom
The top must be thin to let excess water flow over it
questions.explanation: Water exerts pressure horizontally on the dam wall, and this pressure is greatest near the bottom where the column above is tallest. A broad base withstands it.

questions.question: Liquids exert pressure only at the bottom of a container.
questions.explanation: Activity 6.2 shows water spurting from side holes: liquids exert pressure on the sides too — in fact in all directions.

questions.question: In a dam, the horizontal pressure of the stored water on the wall is greatest near the bottom.
questions.explanation: The pressure at any point depends on the height of water above it, so it is largest near the base — which is why the base is built broader.

questions.question: Two pipes of different diameters filled to the same height exert different pressures at the bottom, because they hold different weights of water.
questions.explanation: Activity 6.1 shows equal bulges for equal heights despite different weights of water. Liquid pressure depends on the column height, not the weight held.

questions.question: Which statement about pressure in liquids is NOT correct?
options: Two balloons under equal water columns bulge equally even if the pipes differ in width
The pressure at the bottom of a liquid column rises as the column gets taller
Water in a pipe pushes on the pipe walls, which is why leaks spurt out sideways
A wider column of water gives more pressure at its base than a narrower one of the same height
questions.explanation: Width does not matter — only the height of the column. The remaining three statements are exactly what Activities 6.1 and 6.2 demonstrate.

questions.question: Which observations show that liquids push on the SIDES of their container? (Select all that apply.)
options: Water spurting from holes made in the side of a bottle
Water fountaining out of a leaking joint in a pipe
A balloon bulging at the bottom of a water-filled pipe
A tap giving a strong stream from a rooftop tank
A bag's narrow strap hurting the shoulder
questions.explanation: Side holes and pipe leaks show sideways (wall) pressure. The balloon and tap examples show pressure at the bottom due to column height, and the strap is about solids.

questions.question: Which statements about overhead water tanks are correct? (Select all that apply.)
options: A taller water column gives more pressure at the taps
A wider tank at the same height gives more pressure at the taps
Lower floors receive a stronger stream than higher floors
The height of the tank does not affect the pressure at the taps
questions.explanation: Liquid pressure depends on column height, so raising the tank or being on a lower floor increases tap pressure. Tank width or volume makes no difference.

questions.question: The envelope of air surrounding the Earth is called the
options: stratus layer
hydrosphere
atmosphere
troposphere
questions.explanation: The chapter calls the envelope of air around the Earth the atmosphere; it extends many kilometres above the surface.

questions.question: Which gases does the chapter list as present in atmospheric air?
options: Nitrogen, hydrogen, helium and ozone
Nitrogen, oxygen, argon and carbon dioxide
Oxygen, chlorine, neon and water vapour
Carbon monoxide, oxygen, argon and methane
questions.explanation: Atmospheric air contains nitrogen, oxygen, argon, carbon dioxide and other gases in small quantities.

questions.question: In Activity 6.3, lifting the inverted paper plate is harder when it is covered with the UNFOLDED chart paper. Why?
options: Air pushes on a larger area of sheet, so the total force on it is bigger
The unfolded sheet is heavier, so more effort is needed to lift it
The unfolded sheet sticks to the plate because of static charges
The hole for the stick lets air escape faster from under the plate
questions.explanation: The weight of the sheet is unchanged. The larger area means air exerts a larger total force on the sheet, so more effort is needed — showing air exerts pressure.

questions.question: In Activity 6.3, which quantity is deliberately CHANGED and which is kept the SAME between the two trials?
options: Changed: size of the paper plate; same: length of the stick
Changed: weight of the sheet; same: area of the covering sheet
Changed: area of the covering sheet; same: weight of the sheet
Changed: material of the sheet; same: area of the sheet
questions.explanation: The same chart paper is used folded (small area) and unfolded (large area), so its weight is identical and only the exposed area differs — a fair test of air pressure.

questions.question: The pressure exerted by the air around us is called
options: atmospheric pressure
liquid pressure
wind pressure
static pressure
questions.explanation: Air exerts pressure on all objects; this pressure of the surrounding air is known as atmospheric pressure.

questions.question: A balloon expands in ALL directions when you blow into it. What does this show about the air inside?
options: Air cools inside the balloon and spreads out evenly
Air inside the balloon is heavier than the air outside it
Air pushes only upward, stretching the top of the balloon
Air exerts pressure in all directions on the balloon walls
questions.explanation: The inflating air pushes on every part of the balloon wall, so the balloon grows in all directions — air exerts pressure in all directions.

questions.question: A rubber sucker pressed on a smooth flat surface sticks because
options: the rubber becomes sticky when it is pressed firmly on a surface
outside air pressure is higher than the reduced pressure inside the cup
the surface attracts the rubber through a small electric charge
air trapped inside the cup pushes the sucker against the surface
questions.explanation: Pressing pushes most of the air out of the cup, lowering the pressure inside. The higher atmospheric pressure outside then holds the sucker to the surface.

questions.question: Sucker M is pressed on a smooth flat surface and an identical sucker N on a rough surface. What happens?
options: M sticks but N does not
Both M and N stick
Neither M nor N sticks
N sticks but M does not
questions.explanation: A rough surface lets air leak back under the cup, so the pressure inside is not kept low and N fails to stick. On the smooth surface air stays out, so M sticks.

questions.question: To pull a stuck rubber sucker off a surface, the applied force must
options: overcome the weight of the air column directly above the sucker
overcome the difference between outside and inside air pressure
exceed the force of gravity acting on the rubber of the sucker
be larger than the friction between the rubber and the surface
questions.explanation: The sucker is held by the pressure difference between the atmosphere outside and the low-pressure air inside; the pulling force must beat that difference.

questions.question: The force of the atmospheric air column over a 15 cm × 15 cm area is about
options: 22.5 N, like the weight of a 225 kg object
225 N, like the weight of a 22.5 kg object
2250 N, like the weight of a 225 kg object
2250 N, like the weight of a 2250 kg object
questions.explanation: The chapter says the force over 15 cm × 15 cm is nearly equal to the force of gravity on a 225 kg mass, i.e. about 2250 N.

questions.question: Why are we not crushed by the huge atmospheric pressure acting on us?
options: The atmosphere is too thin near the ground to press on us much
Our skin is strong enough to resist the whole weight of the air column
Air pressure acts only on the top of our heads, which are hard
The pressure inside our body equals the atmospheric pressure and balances it
questions.explanation: The movement of fluids and gases in our tissues and organs creates an internal pressure equal to atmospheric pressure, so the outside push is balanced.

questions.question: The atmosphere extends only a few hundred metres above the surface of the Earth.
questions.explanation: The chapter states that the atmosphere extends up to many kilometres above the Earth's surface.

questions.question: A rubber sucker sticks to a surface because the air pressure outside it is higher than the air pressure inside it.
questions.explanation: Pressing expels most of the air inside, lowering the inside pressure; the greater outside atmospheric pressure then holds the sucker down.

questions.question: Air exerts pressure only downwards, on the upper surfaces of objects.
questions.explanation: Air exerts pressure in all directions, which is why an inflating balloon expands in every direction.

questions.question: Which statements about atmospheric pressure are correct? (Select all that apply.)
options: It acts on all objects around us
It is balanced by the pressure inside our body
It acts only on the upper surface of objects
It is caused by the weight of water in pipes
questions.explanation: Air exerts pressure on all objects and in all directions; our internal body pressure balances it. Water pressure in pipes is liquid pressure, not atmospheric.

questions.question: Predict: in Activity 6.3, the sheet is folded once (half the area) instead of twice (quarter area). Compared with the twice-folded sheet, lifting will be
options: easier, because the sheet is now lighter
harder, because air acts on a bigger sheet area
the same, because the sheet's weight is unchanged
easier, because one fold lets air leak under it
questions.explanation: Effort rises with the area the air pushes on. Half the area is more than a quarter, so lifting is harder than with the twice-folded sheet (but easier than fully unfolded).

questions.topic: Air Flow and Formation of Wind
questions.question: In Activity 6.5, an inflated balloon is joined by a straw to an uninflated one. What happens?
options: Both balloons deflate completely as air escapes through the straw
Air flows from the small balloon into the big one, making it bigger
Nothing happens because the straw is too narrow for air to pass
Air flows into the uninflated balloon until both are nearly equal in size
questions.explanation: Air moves from the higher-pressure inflated balloon to the lower-pressure uninflated one until the pressures (and sizes) are almost equal.

questions.topic: Air Flow and Formation of Wind
questions.question: Why does the air flow between the two balloons in Activity 6.5 eventually STOP?
options: The straw becomes blocked by moisture from breath
The inflated balloon has released all of its air
The air pressure in both balloons becomes equal
The rubber of the smaller balloon cannot stretch further
questions.explanation: Air flows only while there is a pressure difference. When the pressures become equal, the flow stops and both balloons are about the same size.

questions.topic: Air Flow and Formation of Wind
questions.question: Air moves from a region of ______ pressure to a region of ______ pressure.
options: high; low
low; high
warm; cold
equal; unequal
questions.explanation: The balloon activity, the punctured tube and the open balloon all show that air moves from high pressure towards low pressure.

questions.topic: Air Flow and Formation of Wind
questions.question: If we could measure the speed of the escaping air in Activity 6.5, we would find that it is higher when
options: the room temperature is lower than usual
the two balloons are already almost equal in size
the straw joining the balloons is made longer
the pressure difference between the balloons is larger
questions.explanation: The chapter says the speed of air flow is higher if the pressure difference is higher. Near-equal sizes mean a small difference and slow flow.

questions.topic: Air Flow and Formation of Wind
questions.question: When a bicycle tube is punctured, air escapes and the tube collapses. This is because air
options: is pulled out by the weight of the rubber tube itself
moves from the low pressure inside to the higher pressure outside
moves from the high pressure inside to the lower pressure outside
becomes heavier inside the tube and sinks out of the hole
questions.explanation: The air inside the tube is at higher pressure than the atmosphere; it flows out towards the low-pressure region until the tube collapses.

questions.topic: Air Flow and Formation of Wind
questions.question: Which activity best demonstrates that air flows from high to low pressure?
options: Pressing a rubber sucker on a smooth surface and trying to pull it off
Joining an inflated and an uninflated balloon with a straw and watching the sizes change
Lifting an inverted paper plate covered with folded and unfolded sheets
Filling two pipes of different widths with water to the same height
questions.explanation: The balloon-and-straw activity shows air moving from the higher-pressure (inflated) balloon to the lower-pressure one. The others demonstrate atmospheric or liquid pressure.

questions.topic: Air Flow and Formation of Wind
questions.question: Which statement about Activity 6.5 is NOT correct?
options: Air keeps flowing until the inflated balloon is completely empty
Air flows because the inflated balloon has higher pressure
The flow stops when both balloons reach the same pressure
At the end both balloons are almost the same size
questions.explanation: The flow stops when pressures become equal, at which point both balloons are of similar size — the inflated one never empties completely.

questions.topic: Air Flow and Formation of Wind
questions.question: Air flows from a region of higher pressure to a region of lower pressure.
questions.explanation: This is the basic rule shown by the balloon-and-straw activity and the cause of winds.

questions.topic: Air Flow and Formation of Wind
questions.question: What is the main cause of winds blowing?
options: The spinning of clouds high above the ground
The pull of the Moon on the atmosphere
Differences in air pressure between regions
Differences in the amount of dust in the air
questions.explanation: Winds are air moving from high-pressure to low-pressure regions; pressure differences (often from uneven heating) drive them.

questions.topic: Air Flow and Formation of Wind
questions.question: Predict: two balloons inflated to exactly the SAME size are joined by a straw. What will happen?
options: No air will flow, since there is no pressure difference
Air will flow back and forth until both balloons burst
Both balloons will slowly shrink as air escapes through the straw
Air will flow from the left balloon to the right one
questions.explanation: Air moves only when there is a pressure difference. Equal balloons have equal pressure, so there is no flow.

questions.topic: Air Flow and Formation of Wind
questions.question: Which of these are examples of AIR moving from high to low pressure? (Select all that apply.)
options: Air leaving an open inflated balloon
Water flowing from a tap fed by an overhead tank
A punctured bicycle tube collapsing
A balloon bulging at the bottom of a water pipe
questions.explanation: The open balloon and punctured tube both let high-pressure air escape to the lower-pressure surroundings. The other two are about liquid pressure.

questions.topic: Air Flow and Formation of Wind
questions.question: Fig. 6.19 shows pressures of 994 mb, 996 mb, 998 mb and 1008 mb around a cyclone. In which direction do the winds blow?
options: From 996 mb to 998 mb and then on to 1008 mb
From the 994 mb region towards the 1008 mb region
Only along the 998 mb line, neither inward nor outward
From the 1008 mb region towards the 994 mb region
questions.explanation: Air moves from high to low pressure, so winds blow from the 1008 mb outer region inward towards the 994 mb low-pressure centre.

questions.question: During the day, a sea breeze blows from the sea to the land because
options: the sea heats faster, so warm air above it rises and creates low pressure
land heats faster, so warm air above it rises and creates low pressure
the land cools faster, so air above it sinks and creates high pressure
waves push the air above the sea towards the land all day long
questions.explanation: Land heats faster than water. The warm, lighter air over land rises, forming a low-pressure region; air from the higher-pressure sea moves in as a sea breeze.

questions.question: At night the wind blows from the land to the sea. This is called a
options: land breeze
sea breeze
cyclone
mango shower
questions.explanation: At night the water is warmer than the land, so low pressure forms over the sea and air flows from land to sea — a land breeze.

questions.question: Trees along a sea coast are seen bending towards side A on a summer afternoon. Which side is the land, and why?
options: B — the afternoon sea breeze blows from land to sea, bending trees seaward
A — the afternoon sea breeze blows from sea to land, bending trees landward
A — the land breeze blows from the sea towards the land in the afternoon
B — trees always bend away from the land because the land is hotter
questions.explanation: In the afternoon the land is hotter, so low pressure forms over it and the sea breeze blows from the sea to the land. Trees bend in the wind's direction — towards the land, side A.

questions.question: The same coastal trees are observed late at night. Towards which side would the wind now push them?
options: Neither side, because there is never any wind at night on a coast
Towards the land, because a sea breeze blows all day and all night
Towards the sea, because a land breeze now blows from land to sea
Towards the land, because the land is warmer than the sea at night
questions.explanation: At night the land cools faster than the water, so low pressure forms over the warmer sea and the land breeze blows from land to sea.

questions.question: Put the sea-breeze steps in the correct order: (1) air over land rises, (2) land heats faster than sea, (3) low pressure forms over land, (4) air from the sea moves in.
questions.explanation: Heating comes first; the warm, lighter air rises; this leaves low pressure over the land; air from the high-pressure sea then flows in.

questions.question: At night the water is warmer than the land, so a low-pressure area develops above the sea.
questions.explanation: Land cools faster at night; the warmer sea heats the air above it, which rises and leaves low pressure over the sea.

questions.question: During the day, a sea breeze blows from the land towards the sea.
questions.explanation: A sea breeze blows from the SEA to the LAND during the day, because low pressure forms over the heated land.

questions.question: The land breeze and sea breeze are mainly due to
options: the tides raising and lowering the sea level
pressure differences over the land and the sea
the Earth's rotation spinning the coastal air
salt in sea air making it heavier than land air
questions.explanation: Uneven heating of land and sea produces pressure differences, and air moves from high to low pressure — giving sea and land breezes.

questions.question: Which statements about the SEA breeze are correct? (Select all that apply.)
options: It occurs during the day
Warm air over the land rises to create low pressure
It blows from the land towards the sea
It is caused by the sea being warmer than the land
questions.explanation: The sea breeze is a daytime wind from sea to land, driven by warm air rising over the hotter land. The last two describe the night-time land breeze.

questions.question: Suppose on some day the land and the sea were at exactly the same temperature all afternoon. What would you expect?
options: A cyclone, since equal temperatures make air spin quickly
A stronger sea breeze, since equal heating adds more air
A land breeze, since the sea would then be relatively warmer
Little or no breeze, since no pressure difference would form
questions.explanation: Breezes need a pressure difference created by uneven heating. Equal temperatures mean equal pressures, so no breeze forms.

questions.question: Warm air rises because, compared with cooler air, it is
options: wetter
heavier
lighter
saltier
questions.explanation: The chapter explains that air above heated land becomes warmer and lighter, so it rises and creates a low-pressure area.

questions.question: In Activity 6.6, air is blown into the narrow gap between two hanging balloons. What happens?
options: The balloons move towards each other
The balloons move away from each other
The balloons spin around their strings
The balloons rise upwards on their strings
questions.explanation: Blowing between the balloons creates low pressure in the gap; the higher pressure outside pushes them together.

questions.question: Why do the two balloons move together when you blow between them?
options: The strings twist and pull the balloons towards each other
The blown air pushes the balloons sideways and they bounce back together
Breath is warm and makes the balloons expand until they touch
Fast air between them lowers the pressure there, and outside air pushes them in
questions.explanation: High-speed air is accompanied by reduced pressure. With low pressure in the gap and normal pressure outside, the balloons are pushed towards each other.

questions.question: If you blow HARDER between the balloons in Activity 6.6, what changes?
options: They move apart, since harder blowing raises the pressure between them
They stop moving, since the fast air now pushes them apart
They approach each other faster, since the pressure drop is bigger
Nothing changes, since the gap between them is fixed by the stick
questions.explanation: Faster air means an even lower pressure between the balloons, so the push from the outside air is larger and they come together more quickly.

questions.question: What do we infer from the two-balloon activity?
options: High-speed winds are accompanied by increased air pressure
High-speed winds are accompanied by reduced air pressure
Balloons always attract each other when they are inflated
Air pressure does not depend on the speed of the wind
questions.explanation: The chapter concludes that high-speed winds are accompanied by a reduced air pressure — the basis for understanding how storms blow roofs away.

questions.question: Why can high-speed winds blow the roof off a house?
options: Fast wind above lowers the pressure above the roof, while pressure below stays higher
Fast wind presses down on the roof so hard that the walls give way
Fast wind heats the roof, making the metal sheets expand and lift
Fast wind carries dust that piles up on the roof and weighs it down
questions.explanation: Over the roof the fast wind creates low pressure; inside the house the pressure is higher. If the difference is large and the roof weak, the roof is pushed up and away.

questions.question: Why is it safer to keep doors and windows OPEN during a storm with high-speed winds?
options: Open windows let the wind push the roof down more firmly onto the walls
Open doors let the heavy rain flow out instead of collecting on the floor
Wind passing through the house reduces the pressure difference between inside and above the roof
Open doors allow people to escape quickly when the roof blows away
questions.explanation: When the same wind moves through the house as well as over the roof, the pressure inside drops too, reducing the difference that would lift the roof.

questions.question: Which statement about storms and roofs is NOT correct?
options: Roofs are blown off because the wind pushes down on them with great force
Low pressure forms above a roof when fast wind blows over it
A large pressure difference and a weak roof together cause the roof to lift
Letting wind pass through a house helps keep its roof in place
questions.explanation: The roof is lifted from BELOW by the higher inside pressure, because the fast wind lowers the pressure above it — not pushed down by the wind.

questions.question: Why are holes made in large banners and hoardings?
options: So that the printing ink dries faster after the banner is made
So that rainwater can drain away instead of collecting on the cloth
So the banner weighs less and can be hung with thinner ropes
So wind can pass through, reducing the pressure difference and the force on the banner
questions.explanation: A solid banner facing a fast wind experiences a large pressure difference between its two faces and can tear or topple. Holes let air through and reduce this difference.

questions.question: Predict: you hold a strip of paper hanging from your fingers and blow steadily OVER its top surface. The strip will
options: sink, because the blown air presses down on it
rise, because fast air above it lowers the pressure there
stay still, because the air passes above it and not on it
flutter downwards, because moisture in breath makes it heavy
questions.explanation: Fast-moving air above the strip has lower pressure than the still air below it, so the higher pressure below pushes the strip upward.

questions.question: High-speed winds are accompanied by increased air pressure.
questions.explanation: The two-balloon activity shows the opposite: high-speed winds are accompanied by REDUCED air pressure.

questions.question: Keeping doors and windows open during a storm reduces the pressure difference between the inside of a house and the air above its roof.
questions.explanation: Wind moving through the house lowers the inside pressure too, so the difference that could lift the roof is greatly reduced.

questions.question: In Activity 6.6, what is the variable you change by blowing harder, and what responds to it?
options: You change the air speed in the gap; the pressure in the gap responds
You change the pressure in the gap; the balloons' weight responds
You change the balloons' size; the length of the strings responds
You change the room temperature; the air speed in the gap responds
questions.explanation: Blowing harder increases the speed of air in the gap; this lowers the pressure there, which in turn makes the balloons approach faster.

questions.question: Which actions would REDUCE the chance of a roof being blown off in a storm? (Select all that apply.)
options: Opening the doors and windows of the house
Making the roof stronger and firmly fixed
Closing every window tightly to keep the wind out
Making the roof as light as possible
questions.explanation: Opening the house lets wind through and reduces the pressure difference; a strong roof resists lifting. Sealing the house keeps inside pressure high, and a lighter roof lifts more easily.

questions.question: A hoarding WITHOUT holes and one WITH holes face the same high-speed wind. Which is more likely to be damaged, and why?
options: The one with holes — the holes weaken the cloth so it tears
The one without holes — a bigger pressure difference acts across it
Both equally — the wind speed is the same for both of them
The one with holes — more wind can get inside and push it
questions.explanation: With no path for air to pass through, a large pressure difference builds across the solid hoarding, producing a big force. Holes let air through and reduce this difference.

questions.question: When land gets heated, warm moist air rises and creates a low-pressure area. What happens next?
options: The warm air comes straight back down to fill the gap it left
The low pressure pulls the clouds down to the ground as fog
Cooler air from surrounding high-pressure areas flows in to take its place
The surrounding air also rises, leaving the whole area empty
questions.explanation: Air moves from high to low pressure, so cooler air flows in; it is heated, rises in turn, and a continuous circulation of wind results.

questions.question: Why does rising warm air form clouds?
options: It freezes instantly at any height above the ground
It compresses and heats, so the moisture in it boils into vapour
It mixes with dust high up, which turns the air white
It expands and cools, so the moisture in it condenses into droplets
questions.explanation: As the rising air expands, it cools; the water vapour in it condenses into water droplets, which form clouds.

questions.question: According to the chapter, a storm is
options: a spinning system of winds over the ocean
strong winds accompanied by rain
any day with heavy rainfall and no wind
a flash of lightning followed by thunder
questions.explanation: The strong winds accompanied by rain are called a storm. A spinning system is a cyclone; a storm with lightning and thunder is a thunderstorm.

questions.question: Why are storms more frequent in India than in many other places?
options: India is far from any ocean, so air over it heats very quickly
India is cold and dry, so winds blow strongly from the mountains
India has many rivers, which push the air upwards along their banks
India is hot, humid and tropical, giving plenty of warm moist rising air
questions.explanation: Storms need warm, moist air that rises. Hot, humid, tropical regions like India provide these conditions, so storms are more frequent.

questions.question: Under certain conditions, water droplets in a rising cloud turn into ice particles. This happens because
options: lightning freezes the droplets as it passes through the cloud
the rising air is squeezed so hard that the water solidifies
the air rises to great heights where the temperature is very low
salt from the sea mixes with the droplets and makes them solid
questions.explanation: When warm air rises to great heights, the low temperature there converts the water droplets into ice particles.

questions.question: Arrange in order: (1) droplets merge into heavier drops, (2) warm moist air rises, (3) rain, hail or snow falls, (4) air expands, cools and vapour condenses.
questions.explanation: Air rises first; as it expands and cools, vapour condenses into droplets; droplets merge into heavier drops; these fall as rain, hail or snow.

questions.question: Rising air expands and cools, which makes the moisture in it condense into water droplets.
questions.explanation: This is how clouds form: expansion on rising lowers the temperature, and the water vapour condenses.

questions.question: Storms are more frequent in cold, dry regions than in hot, humid, tropical regions.
questions.explanation: It is the reverse: hot, humid, tropical regions like India have more frequent storms because of abundant warm, moist rising air.

questions.question: Which statement about storm formation is NOT correct?
options: Water droplets merge into heavier drops that fall as rain, hail or snow
Warm moist air is lighter and rises, creating low pressure
Cooler air from high-pressure regions flows in to replace rising air
Rising air is compressed and heats up, so its moisture evaporates
questions.explanation: Rising air EXPANDS and COOLS, which makes moisture condense — not compress and evaporate. The other three statements are correct steps.

questions.question: According to the chapter's Snapshots, which are important requirements for the formation of thunderstorms? (Select all that apply.)
options: Moisture in the air
Strong winds
Cold, dry air
Calm, still weather
questions.explanation: The Snapshots list moisture and strong winds as the important requirements. Cold dry air and calm conditions do not produce thunderstorms.

questions.question: Why does the chapter describe the wind in a developing storm as a CONTINUOUS circulation?
options: The Earth's rotation keeps pushing the same air round and round
The air rises once and then spreads out and never returns to the ground
The air that flows in to replace rising air is itself heated and rises in turn
The clouds pull the air up and the rain pushes it back down
questions.explanation: Cooler air flows into the low-pressure area, gets heated, and rises too; more air flows in, and so on — a continuous process of wind circulation.

questions.question: Predict: on a hot day the rising air over a region is almost completely DRY. What is likely?
options: Heavy rain, since dry air cools faster than moist air when it rises
Wind may form, but few clouds, since there is little moisture to condense
A thunderstorm, since dry air rubs together more and charges quickly
No wind at all, since only moist air can rise and create low pressure
questions.explanation: Heating still makes the air rise and creates pressure differences (wind), but clouds and rain need water vapour to condense; dry air gives few clouds.

questions.question: What causes electric charges to develop inside storm clouds?
options: Strong up-and-down winds make water droplets and ice particles rub together
Sunlight striking the top of the cloud knocks charges off the droplets
Rain falling from the cloud carries charge up from the ground
The cloud rubs against mountains as it moves across the sky
questions.explanation: Strong winds blowing upwards and downwards cause rubbing between water droplets and ice particles; as learnt in 'Exploring Forces', rubbing produces static charge.

questions.question: Inside a thundercloud, where do the positively and negatively charged particles collect?
options: Positive and negative charges stay evenly mixed throughout the cloud
Heavier positive water droplets go up; lighter negative ice particles stay low
Lighter positive ice particles go up; heavier negative water droplets stay low
All charges move to the edges of the cloud, leaving the centre neutral
questions.explanation: The positively charged lighter ice particles move to the upper part of the cloud and the negatively charged heavier water droplets occupy the lower part — a charge separation.

questions.question: When the negatively charged lower part of a cloud moves near the ground, the ground and objects on it become
options: positively charged
negatively charged
electrically neutral
insulated from charge
questions.explanation: The negative charge at the cloud base induces a positive charge on the ground and nearby objects such as trees and buildings.

questions.question: Normally, air behaves as an electrical
options: battery
conductor
magnet
insulator
questions.explanation: Air normally acts as an insulator and does not let opposite charges meet. Only when charge build-up is very large does this property break down.

questions.question: Lightning occurs when
options: the air between the cloud and ground becomes completely dry and heats up
the charge build-up becomes so large that air's insulation breaks down and charges flow suddenly
sunlight passes through ice particles at the top of a storm cloud
two clouds collide physically and their water droplets are squeezed out
questions.explanation: When the accumulated charge is very large, the insulating property of air fails and a sudden flow of charges takes place, producing a bright flash — lightning.

questions.question: What produces the sound of thunder?
options: Lightning rapidly heats the air, which expands and makes a loud sound
Clouds bang into each other high above the ground
Hailstones striking each other inside the cloud
Rain hitting the ground at very high speed all at once
questions.explanation: Lightning heats the surrounding air rapidly; the air expands suddenly and produces the loud sound we hear as thunder.

questions.question: A storm accompanied by lightning and thunder is called a
options: cyclone
thunderstorm
sea breeze
storm surge
questions.explanation: The chapter defines a thunderstorm as a storm accompanied by lightning and thunder.

questions.question: Would lightning occur if air and clouds were good conductors of electricity?
options: Yes — lightning depends only on how much water is present in the cloud
Yes — a conductor would carry the charges faster, making lightning more frequent
No — charges would leak away continuously and never build up enough for a sudden flow
No — conductors cannot hold any water droplets, so no clouds would form
questions.explanation: Lightning needs a large build-up of separated charge, which is possible only because air insulates. If air conducted, charges would flow away steadily and no sudden discharge would occur.

questions.question: Where can lightning occur?
options: Only inside a single cloud, where the charges are separated
Only between a cloud and the ground, never inside clouds
Only between two different clouds, never near the ground
Within a cloud, between clouds, or between a cloud and the ground
questions.explanation: Lightning can occur as opposite charges meet within a cloud, between clouds, or between a cloud and the ground.

questions.question: Which statement about charges in a thundercloud is NOT correct?
options: Positively charged ice particles occupy the upper part of the cloud
Negatively charged ice particles rise to the top of the cloud
Negatively charged water droplets occupy the lower part of the cloud
Rubbing between droplets and ice particles produces the charges
questions.explanation: The ice particles are POSITIVELY charged and lighter, so they rise. The negative charge is on the heavier water droplets, which stay lower.

questions.question: The chapter links charging in clouds to which earlier idea from the chapter 'Exploring Forces'?
options: Magnets attract objects made of iron from a distance
Heavier objects fall faster than lighter ones
Forces act in pairs of equal size and opposite direction
Rubbing two objects against each other charges them
questions.explanation: In 'Exploring Forces' students learnt that rubbing two objects charges them; here, droplets and ice particles rubbing in strong winds become charged.

questions.question: The positively charged lighter ice particles collect in the lower part of a thundercloud.
questions.explanation: The lighter positive ice particles move UP to the upper part; the heavier negative water droplets occupy the lower part.

questions.question: Thunder is produced because lightning rapidly heats the air around it, making the air expand suddenly.
questions.explanation: The sudden expansion of rapidly heated air produces the loud sound called thunder.

questions.question: Which statements about lightning are correct? (Select all that apply.)
options: It is a sudden flow of electric charges
It requires air to be a good conductor
It happens when the charge build-up breaks down air's insulating property
It occurs only between a cloud and the ground
questions.explanation: Lightning is a sudden flow of charges that occurs when air's insulation breaks down under a very large charge build-up. Air is normally an insulator, and lightning can occur within or between clouds too.

questions.question: Put the lightning process in order: (1) sudden flow of charges, (2) up-and-down winds rub droplets and ice, (3) charge separation in cloud, (4) air's insulation breaks down.
questions.explanation: Rubbing creates charges; they separate (positive up, negative down); when the build-up is large enough, air's insulation fails; then the charges flow suddenly as lightning.

questions.topic: Local Thunderstorms, Lightning Safety and Conductors
questions.question: Pre-monsoon thunderstorms known as 'Kalboishakhi' occur in
options: West Bengal, Bihar and Jharkhand
Kerala, Karnataka and Tamil Nadu
Assam, Meghalaya and Tripura
Punjab, Haryana and Rajasthan
questions.explanation: The 'A step further' box names Kalboishakhi as the local thunderstorms of West Bengal, Bihar and Jharkhand.

questions.topic: Local Thunderstorms, Lightning Safety and Conductors
questions.question: The local pre-monsoon thunderstorm of Assam is called
options: Amphan
Kalboishakhi
Mango shower
Bordoisila
questions.explanation: In Assam these isolated thunderstorms are known as Bordoisila. Kalboishakhi is the name in Bengal, Bihar and Jharkhand; Amphan was a cyclone.

questions.topic: Local Thunderstorms, Lightning Safety and Conductors
questions.question: Why are the pre-monsoon thunderstorms of Kerala, Karnataka and Tamil Nadu called 'mango showers'?
options: They happen when mango trees flower
They occur only in mango orchards
They support the ripening of mangoes
Their raindrops are the size of mangoes
questions.explanation: The chapter says they are called mango showers because they support the ripening of mangoes.

questions.topic: Local Thunderstorms, Lightning Safety and Conductors
questions.question: Local thunderstorms in Karnataka are said to help the growth of which crop?
options: Rice
Coffee
Wheat
Cotton
questions.explanation: The box notes that local thunderstorms in Karnataka help in the growth of coffee plants.

questions.topic: Local Thunderstorms, Lightning Safety and Conductors
questions.question: Kalboishakhi and Bordoisila occur BEFORE the monsoon arrives. How does this timing help farmers?
options: It helps kharif crops to grow
It dries the fields before sowing
It delays the main monsoon rain
It prevents floods in the monsoon
questions.explanation: These pre-monsoon thunderstorms bring rain that helps the kharif crops to grow.

questions.topic: Local Thunderstorms, Lightning Safety and Conductors
questions.question: Which is the recommended way to protect yourself when caught outdoors during lightning?
options: Lie down flat on the ground so that you are as low as possible
Stand under the tallest tree nearby so that the tree takes the strike
Find a low-lying open area, crouch down and minimise contact with the ground
Open an umbrella with a metal rod to deflect the lightning away
questions.explanation: The chapter advises staying away from tall objects, crouching in a low open area with minimal ground contact, and not lying flat.

questions.topic: Local Thunderstorms, Lightning Safety and Conductors
questions.question: Why should you NOT lie down flat on the ground during lightning?
options: Lying flat maximises your contact with the ground
Lying flat makes you the tallest object in the area
Lying flat attracts positive charges from the cloud
Lying flat prevents you from seeing the lightning
questions.explanation: The advice is to crouch and minimise contact with the ground; lying flat increases ground contact, which the chapter warns against.

questions.topic: Local Thunderstorms, Lightning Safety and Conductors
questions.question: Which of these is NOT a safe practice during lightning?
options: Keeping away from tall objects
Getting out of water if you are in it
Staying inside a bus or a car
Using an umbrella with a metallic rod
questions.explanation: The chapter says to AVOID an umbrella with a metallic rod. Leaving water, staying in a vehicle and avoiding tall objects are all recommended.

questions.topic: Local Thunderstorms, Lightning Safety and Conductors
questions.question: During a thunderstorm, is it safer to be inside a car?
options: No — a metal car attracts lightning and must be left at once
Yes — the chapter says you are comparatively safer inside a bus or car
No — cars are only safe if parked under a tall tree for shelter
Yes — but only if all the windows are rolled down for air flow
questions.explanation: The chapter states that if you are inside a bus or a car, you are comparatively safer during lightning.

questions.topic: Local Thunderstorms, Lightning Safety and Conductors
questions.question: A lightning conductor is a
options: metallic rod with a pointed end above the building and the other end buried in the ground
rubber rod placed on the roof to insulate the building from the clouds
glass rod fixed to the wall to reflect lightning back into the sky
metallic rod kept inside the building to store the electric charge safely
questions.explanation: A lightning conductor is a metallic rod installed along the building walls; its pointed end sits above the highest point and the other end is buried deep in the ground.

questions.topic: Local Thunderstorms, Lightning Safety and Conductors
questions.question: How does a lightning conductor protect a building?
options: It stops clouds from becoming charged above the building
It provides an easy path for electric charges to pass into the ground
It absorbs the lightning's heat so that the building stays cool
It pushes the storm clouds away from the top of the building
questions.explanation: The rod offers an easy path for charges to flow to the ground, so the lightning's charge bypasses the building itself.

questions.topic: Local Thunderstorms, Lightning Safety and Conductors
questions.question: During lightning you should lie down flat on the ground to be as low as possible.
questions.explanation: The chapter says do NOT lie down flat; crouch in a low open area and minimise contact with the ground.

questions.topic: Local Thunderstorms, Lightning Safety and Conductors
questions.question: One end of a lightning conductor is kept higher than the highest point of the building.
questions.explanation: The pointed end of the metallic rod is placed above the building's highest point; the other end is buried deep in the ground.

questions.topic: Local Thunderstorms, Lightning Safety and Conductors
questions.question: Which actions are SAFE during lightning? (Select all that apply.)
options: Get out of water if you are in it
Crouch down in a low-lying open area
Stand under the tallest tree for shelter
Open an umbrella with a metal rod
questions.explanation: Leaving water and crouching low are recommended. Tall objects and metallic umbrella rods should be avoided.

questions.topic: Local Thunderstorms, Lightning Safety and Conductors
questions.question: Match the local thunderstorm to its region: Kalboishakhi, Bordoisila, mango showers.
options: Kerala/Karnataka/Tamil Nadu; Assam; Bengal/Bihar/Jharkhand
Assam; Bengal/Bihar/Jharkhand; Kerala/Karnataka/Tamil Nadu
Bengal/Bihar/Jharkhand; Assam; Kerala/Karnataka/Tamil Nadu
Bengal/Bihar/Jharkhand; Kerala/Karnataka/Tamil Nadu; Assam
questions.explanation: Kalboishakhi belongs to West Bengal, Bihar and Jharkhand; Bordoisila to Assam; mango showers to Kerala, Karnataka and Tamil Nadu.

questions.topic: Local Thunderstorms, Lightning Safety and Conductors
questions.question: Which features correctly describe a lightning conductor? (Select all that apply.)
options: It is a metallic rod fixed along the building's walls
Its pointed end is kept above the building's highest point
It is made of rubber to insulate the building
It is kept inside the building to store the charge
questions.explanation: A lightning conductor is a metallic rod whose pointed end rises above the building and whose other end is buried in the ground, giving charges an easy path to earth.

questions.question: Cyclones are large storms that form over
options: frozen polar ice
cold mountain peaks
dry desert sands
warm ocean waters
questions.explanation: Cyclones form over warm ocean waters, where warm, moist air rises from the heated sea surface.

questions.question: When water vapour in rising air condenses into raindrops, what happens to the heat?
options: Heat is absorbed, cooling the air so that it sinks back down
Heat is released, warming the air further so it rises even more
Heat is destroyed, so the temperature of the air stays the same
Heat is turned into lightning that flashes within the cloud
questions.explanation: Evaporation takes up heat; condensation gives it back. The released heat warms the ascending air, making it rise further and lowering the pressure even more.

questions.question: Which pair of statements about water is used in the chapter to explain cyclone growth?
options: Both evaporation and condensation take heat from the air
Evaporation releases heat; condensation takes up heat
Both evaporation and condensation release heat to the air
Evaporation takes up heat; condensation releases heat back
questions.explanation: Water absorbs heat to evaporate; when the vapour condenses into raindrops, that heat is released into the atmosphere, fuelling the rising air.

questions.question: What makes the moving air in a developing cyclone SPIN?
options: The heat of the Sun
The Moon's gravity
The Earth's rotation
The salt in sea water
questions.explanation: The chapter says Earth's rotation causes the moving air to spin, producing high-speed winds revolving around a very low-pressure centre.

questions.question: How does a storm develop into a cyclone?
options: Condensation releases heat, air rises faster, pressure falls further, more air rushes in and spins
Lightning heats the air so much that it spins rapidly around the storm
Rain cools the sea, which pushes the storm clouds upward in a spiral
Strong land breezes blow the storm out to sea, where it starts to rotate
questions.explanation: Heat released by condensing vapour warms the rising air, which rises more and deepens the low pressure; surrounding air rushes in, rises too, and Earth's rotation makes it spin — repeating until a cyclone forms.

questions.question: The centre of a cyclone, where the pressure is lowest, is called its
options: funnel
core
surge
eye
questions.explanation: The region of lowest pressure at the centre of a cyclone is known as the eye of the cyclone.

questions.question: What is the weather like at the EYE of a cyclone?
options: Light drizzle with moderate winds blowing in a circle
The strongest winds and heaviest rain of the whole cyclone
Calm winds, while the surrounding region has strong winds and heavy rain
Snowfall, because the eye is the coldest part of the cyclone
questions.explanation: At the eye the wind is calm, but the region surrounding it experiences strong winds and heavy rainfall.

questions.question: Why does a cyclone gradually lose its strength after reaching land?
options: The land is colder than the ocean surface
Its source of moist air is cut off
Trees and buildings block its winds
The Earth rotates more slowly over land
questions.explanation: A cyclone is fed by warm, moist air from the ocean. Over land this supply is cut off, so the cyclone weakens.

questions.question: 'If the Earth stopped rotating, would cyclones still form?' Using the chapter, the best answer is
options: Warm moist air could still rise, but without rotation the winds would not spin into a cyclone
Yes, exactly as now, because cyclones depend only on how warm the ocean is
No, because without rotation water could not evaporate from the ocean
Yes, and they would be stronger, because nothing would slow the rising air
questions.explanation: Rising air and low pressure come from heating and condensation, but it is Earth's rotation that makes the inrushing air spin. Without spin, the spinning system we call a cyclone would not form.

questions.question: The eye of a cyclone is the region of lowest pressure, where the winds are calm.
questions.explanation: The eye is the calm, lowest-pressure centre, surrounded by strong winds and heavy rain.

questions.question: A cyclone gains strength after reaching land because the land is warmer than the sea.
questions.explanation: A cyclone LOSES strength over land because its supply of warm, moist ocean air is cut off.

questions.question: Which of these are needed for a cyclone to form, according to the chapter? (Select all that apply.)
options: Warm ocean water
The Earth's rotation
Cold, dry air over land
A lightning conductor
questions.explanation: Cyclones need warm, moist air rising from warm oceans and Earth's rotation to make the winds spin. Cold dry land air weakens cyclones; conductors are for lightning.

questions.question: In Fig. 6.19 the pressure values read 1008 mb, 998 mb, 996 mb and 994 mb. Where is 994 mb found?
options: Over the land far from the sea
At the outer edge of the cyclone
At the centre of the cyclone
Spread evenly across the whole cyclone
questions.explanation: Pressure falls towards the centre of a cyclone; the lowest value (994 mb) is at the eye and the highest (1008 mb) at the outside.

questions.question: Which statement about cyclones is NOT correct?
options: The eye of a cyclone experiences the strongest winds and heaviest rain
Cyclones form over warm ocean waters from rising moist air
Heat released by condensing water vapour makes the air rise further
Earth's rotation makes the inrushing air spin around the centre
questions.explanation: The eye is CALM; strong winds and heavy rain are in the region around it. The other statements are correct descriptions of cyclone formation.

questions.question: During evaporation water releases heat, and during condensation it absorbs heat.
questions.explanation: It is the reverse: water TAKES UP heat to evaporate and RELEASES it when the vapour condenses — this released heat fuels the cyclone.

questions.question: The Amphan cyclone of 2020 had peak wind speeds of about
options: 500 km/h
27 km/h
120 km/h
270 km/h
questions.explanation: The chapter gives Amphan's peak wind speed as 270 km/h as an example of how destructive cyclones can be.

questions.question: Strong cyclone winds push ocean water towards the shore, creating a wall of water about
options: 30–120 metres high
3–12 metres high
3–12 centimetres high
0.3–1.2 metres high
questions.explanation: This surge of water can be as high as 3–12 metres and can flood coastal areas and even places far from the sea.

questions.question: How can seawater that rushes inland during a cyclone harm farming?
options: Its salt makes the soil less fertile, affecting crops
It washes away all the insects that pollinate crops
It cools the soil so much that seeds cannot sprout
It brings sand that makes the soil drain too quickly
questions.explanation: The chapter says seawater damages farmland and that the salt in it can make the soil less fertile.

questions.question: Which organisation issues cyclone weather reports, alerts and warnings in India?
options: Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO)
India Meteorological Department (IMD)
National Highways Authority of India (NHAI)
Indian Council of Agricultural Research (ICAR)
questions.explanation: The India Meteorological Department (IMD) constantly monitors cyclones and thunderstorms and issues alerts and warnings.

questions.question: How do weather monitoring satellites help reduce the impact of cyclones?
options: They cool the ocean water so that cyclones cannot form
They blow the cyclones back out to sea with powerful winds
They let us track cyclones and predict their paths in advance
They remove the moisture from the air above the cyclone
questions.explanation: Satellites allow cyclones to be tracked and their paths predicted, so warnings can be issued and people can prepare.

questions.question: What should you do during a cyclone if you live in a cyclone-prone area?
options: Drive out of town along the coastal road
Go to the beach to watch the storm surge
Climb onto the roof to stay above the flood water
Move quickly to a nearby designated cyclone shelter
questions.explanation: The chapter advises keeping an emergency kit ready and, during a cyclone, moving quickly to a nearby designated cyclone shelter.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT listed in the chapter as an effect of cyclones?
options: Rivers overflowing due to heavy rainfall
Volcanic eruptions along the coast
Landslides triggered by heavy rain
Power outages lasting for days
questions.explanation: The chapter lists flooding, overflowing rivers, landslides, contaminated water, damaged farmland, blocked roads and power outages — not volcanic eruptions.

questions.question: The salt in seawater that floods farmland during a cyclone can make the soil less fertile.
questions.explanation: Seawater rushing inland damages farmland, and its salt reduces soil fertility, affecting crops.

questions.question: Cyclone Amphan in 2020 had peak wind speeds of about 120 km/h.
questions.explanation: The chapter gives Amphan's peak wind speed as 270 km/h.

questions.question: Which are effects of a cyclone described in the chapter? (Select all that apply.)
options: Flooding of coastal areas by a surge of seawater
Landslides triggered by heavy rainfall
Lower atmospheric pressure everywhere on Earth
An increase in the fertility of farmland
questions.explanation: Storm surges flood coasts and heavy rain triggers landslides. Cyclones do not lower pressure worldwide, and seawater makes soil LESS fertile.

questions.question: Why is it often difficult for help to reach cyclone-affected areas?
options: Rescue vehicles cannot run in low pressure
The eye of the cyclone stays over the area
The IMD stops issuing reports after landfall
Roads get blocked by fallen trees and debris
questions.explanation: The chapter notes that roads may get blocked due to fallen trees and debris, making it difficult for help to reach affected areas.

questions.question: During a cyclone, rivers may overflow and landslides may be triggered. The common cause given in the chapter is
options: the low pressure at the eye lifting the water
the Earth's rotation shaking the ground
the heavy rainfall that accompanies the cyclone
the lightning striking the river banks
questions.explanation: The heavy rainfall which accompanies a cyclone may cause rivers to overflow and can trigger landslides.

questions.question: A cyclone has weakened after crossing the coast, yet the chapter says it can still cause damage lasting months. Which is the best reason?
options: Surge flooding, salt-damaged soil, blocked roads and power cuts persist long after the winds die
The cyclone keeps its full ocean strength for weeks after crossing the coast
The eye of the cyclone stays fixed over the town and never moves away
The weakened cyclone turns into a thunderstorm that lasts for months
questions.explanation: Even as the winds weaken over land, the trail of destruction — floods, contaminated water, less fertile soil, blocked roads and power outages — takes months or years to repair.
